opus-5.5.text:
Well, thanks for having me. I think the core challenge is that our networks only learn the features they need to discriminate among the classes in the training data. If you train an image classifier to tell cats from dogs, it learns whatever is sufficient to separate those two, and it has no reason to represent anything else about the world. So when something genuinely novel shows up, say a raccoon, the network may simply not have the features that would let it notice the novelty. The raccoon gets mapped into the same representation space and often lands right in the middle of the cat or dog region with high confidence.

We've seen this empirically. A lot of the anomaly detection work my group has done suggests that what these detectors really measure is something like "familiarity" rather than "novelty." The network can tell you when it sees a strong activation of the patterns it already knows, but it has a hard time telling you that something is missing or that something new is present. A low familiarity score can come from many causes, and the detector can't really distinguish them.

With large language models it gets even harder, because it's not even clear what the training distribution is. These models are trained on a large fraction of the internet, so the question "is this query out of distribution?" becomes kind of ill-posed. Nearly any query will resemble something in the training data on the surface. The more relevant question is whether the model actually has the knowledge or competence to answer it. That's more a question of epistemic uncertainty: does the model know what it doesn't know? Right now these systems are poorly calibrated in that sense. They'll produce fluent, confident text whether or not there's any real knowledge behind it.

So I'd say the main challenge is representational. If we want systems that can detect their own ignorance, we need them to learn richer representations than the minimum required for the training task, perhaps through self-supervised learning or by building in some notion of what a complete explanation of an input looks like. Then the system can notice when part of the input isn't explained. And for high-stakes deployments, we have to pair that with good engineering: monitoring, abstention, and human oversight. We should expect novelty detection to be imperfect and design the overall system to be robust to that.

r001.rationale: It says the network may lack features for a novel raccoon, which can then land in a familiar cat or dog region with high confidence.

r002.rationale: It does not propose that extensive training variability could give unfamiliar objects distinguishable representations; it instead emphasizes the limits of current representations.

r003.rationale: It does not ask whether training-data variability can be mapped to identify missing forms of variation.

r004.rationale: It does not connect missing training-data variability with identifying underrepresented subcommunities for fairness.

r005.rationale: It does not express a view about needing access to LLM training data for fairness research.

r006.rationale: It does not express a view about needing access to LLM training data for explanation research.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, thanks for having me. I think the fundamental challenge is that "out of distribution" is a negative definition. We know what the training distribution looks like, at least in the sense that we have samples from it, but the space of everything else is essentially infinite and unstructured. So you're being asked to recognize membership in a set you've only ever seen one side of.

In the classic supervised setting, the way I like to frame it is that a classifier is really answering the question, "given that this input came from one of my known classes, which one is it?" It's a conditional question. And neural networks are extremely good at answering it, but the softmax output gives you no information about whether the premise holds. You can show a cat-versus-dog classifier a picture of a truck and it will tell you with ninety-eight percent confidence that it's a dog. That overconfidence isn't a bug in the training procedure, it's a consequence of what the model was asked to do. Nothing in the loss function ever rewards it for saying "I don't know."

So the first challenge is just getting a signal that's separate from the class decision. People have tried a lot of things: looking at the magnitude of activations, fitting density models in the feature space, training with auxiliary outlier data, ensembles, and so on. My own view is that the most principled approaches treat this as a kind of anomaly detection on the representation, where you're estimating how far a new input is from the regions where you actually have data. But the deep representation itself was shaped by the classification objective, so it may have thrown away exactly the features you'd need to notice that something is strange. The features that distinguish cats from dogs aren't necessarily the ones that distinguish dogs from trucks.

The second challenge, which I think is underappreciated, is that there are really different kinds of novelty. There's the novel class, something you've never seen a category for. There's the covariate shift case, where it's a familiar class but the imaging conditions or the sensor or the population has changed. And there's the adversarial case, where someone is deliberately constructing inputs to sit in a region of the input space that the model handles badly. Those require quite different responses from the system, and a single "OOD score" tends to conflate them.

Now with large language models it gets harder in an interesting way, because the notion of distribution becomes very slippery. The pretraining corpus is so broad that almost any natural language query is, in some superficial sense, in distribution. The model has seen text about nearly everything. What it hasn't necessarily seen is the particular combination of facts, or the particular reasoning chain, that a query demands. So the out-of-distribution event isn't at the level of the surface form of the input, it's at the level of the knowledge or the competence required. And that's much harder to detect, because the model can produce perfectly fluent, well-formed text whether or not it actually knows the answer. Fluency is in distribution even when the content isn't.

I think this is really the core of the hallucination problem. If you asked me to put it in one sentence, I'd say the challenge is that we want the system to know the boundaries of its own competence, and we've trained it in a way that never required it to learn where those boundaries are. There's some encouraging work on calibration, on having the model estimate its own uncertainty, on retrieval-based approaches where you can at least check whether supporting evidence exists. But fundamentally I think we need to move toward systems that have an explicit model of what they know, rather than hoping that a confidence number falls out as a side effect of next-token prediction.

r001.rationale: The response explains that an unfamiliar truck can still receive a confident familiar class label, and that the model may fail to flag inputs as anomalous. This communicates how an input outside the training regions can map to a familiar representation.

r002.rationale: The response does not hypothesize that extensive training variability could give LLMs, particularly image models, distinguishable representations of unfamiliar objects.

r003.rationale: The response does not ask whether training-data variability can be mapped to find missing forms of variation.

r004.rationale: The response does not connect missing training-data variability with identifying underrepresented subcommunities for fairness.

r005.rationale: The response does not state that fairness research on LLMs requires access to training data.

r006.rationale: The response does not state that explanation research on LLMs requires access to training data.

astra-6.text:
I think the central challenge is that a neural network can be very confident even when it’s being asked about something far outside its training experience. So we can’t simply look at the confidence of its prediction and say, “Well, if that’s high, this must be a familiar case.”

And with language models, there’s another complication: what exactly do we mean by out of distribution? A question can use perfectly familiar words and still require knowledge or reasoning that the model doesn’t have. Conversely, a question that looks unusual may be something it can answer quite well. So detecting novelty and detecting when the model is likely to fail are related problems, but they’re not identical.

What we really want is a system that can recognize when it lacks a reliable basis for an answer and then ask for clarification, seek additional information, or abstain. The hard part is making that recognition reliable for the kinds of unexpected inputs we didn’t anticipate when we built the detector.

r001.rationale: The response says confidence can remain high outside training experience, but does not explain that variation along unseen dimensions may map to familiar representations.

r003.rationale: It does not ask whether training-data variability can be mapped to find missing forms of variation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the central challenge is that a neural network can be very confident even when it’s operating outside the conditions under which it was trained. So confidence alone doesn’t tell us whether a prediction is trustworthy.

And “out of distribution” is not a single, well-defined thing. A query might look quite different from the training data and still be easy to answer correctly. Another query might look completely familiar but require knowledge or reasoning the model doesn’t have. With LLMs, that distinction is especially difficult because a fluent answer can hide the failure.

So what we really want to detect is when the model’s competence breaks down. Can we recognize those cases reliably enough that the system can abstain, ask for clarification, or seek additional information? The hard part is making that work for failures we didn’t anticipate when we built the detector.
